- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast peaks, especially after spikes.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.33) or volatile, model often underestimates or misses downward trends; increase downward bias or add early warning signals.
- Model frequently overreacts to short-term sentiment shifts — especially when sentiment spikes to 1.00 — leading to exaggerated overshoots; apply dampening factor to high-sentiment forecasts.
- Mean reversion is strong in early 30d forecasts — model often fails to correct from recent highs/lows; adjust forecasts toward historical mean if sentiment is neutral or mixed.
- Forecasts with sentiment history showing high volatility (alternating 0.33/1.00) show erratic behavior — avoid extreme outliers; cap or smooth extremes unless sentiment confirms trend.
- If sentiment is stable (e.g., 0.67 for 5+ days), model should align with historical mean; if sentiment shifts, adjust forecast horizon to reflect new sentiment direction.
- Overshoots after sentiment spikes (e.g., 1.00 → 1.00 → 1.00) are common — reduce forecast by 15–30% for next 3–5 days unless confirmed by new data.
- Model underestimates true outcomes when sentiment is low but price is rising — reverse bias if sentiment is low but price is trending up.
- If sentiment is high but price is falling, model often fails to recognize reversal — add early correction signal if sentiment >0.67 and price drops >10% from peak.
